Title: Golden Son (Red Rising Saga, #2)
Author: Pierce Brown
My Review:
I've decided I want to enjoy the things I read, and not suffer through them. The more I think about the first book, the more I have issues with people's claim that it's an "adult" series. The aspects that supposedly make the series more dark and mature, like sexual violence, wartime brutality, and slavery, actually reveal its lack of maturity.

Rape is presented for shock value, then quickly turned into a strategic tool when Darrow uses it to gain Tactus’ loyalty. Yes I was shocked when it was revealed that Tactus was raping women. And I was more shocked when Darrow became friends with the rapist (after punishing him, of course). A protagonist who weaponizes trauma for his goals isn’t someone I feel compelled to root for. The sexual assaults are just used as plot devices with no follow-up other than saying "people do bad things in wartime". There was also a weird thing in the first book where Darrow sees a Pink being mistreated and frees her from sexual captivity, which also feels hollow. It's really just there to make us root for Darrow.

The series sets up a vast world that could be very interesting and nuanced, yet the implementation is so underbaked. The structure of the caste system could be a great opportunity to interrogate the society and the characters within, yet nobody ever meaningfully critiques it. Golds, who are the oppressors, never question their privilege, and they are never prompted to question it by others, either. All the central characters are Golds, so why should we care? The system remains unchallenged, and Darrow himself seems unconcerned at times.

The pieces are all there, but it's just not working. It's like if Remy only ate the strawberry and the cheese separately, and never tried them together.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring (The Lord of the Rings, #1)
Author: J.R.R. Tolkien
My Review:
June 2020 review:
you need a good mental compass to navigate all the places they go. or consult the maps.

January 2026 review:
Before revisiting Fellowship of the Ring, I thought that much like rewatching the movies, I would come to realize that these books are perfect masterpieces that only get better with each read. And while I did enjoy this first volume more this time, I still agree with my last review; the story is windy and often confusing, both in the actual journey of the fellowship and the worldbuilding. The depth of middle-earth's lore is a double-edged sword. The world feels very lived-in with great history and culture, but the specificity of place-names and lineages is overwhelming and often not necessary outside of an appendix or glossary.

Since reading the books for the first time in 2020, I've rewatched the films multiple times, watched two seasons of The Rings of Power, skimmed the Silmarillion, and read lots and lots of neat tidbits and whatever of lore. And I think it greatly contributed to my increased enjoyment when reading passages where before I might've glossed over them. I know who the Númenóreans are now. And Elendil and Celebrimor and others. In my mind-movie Elrond and Galadriel switch back and forth between their original and younger actors.

I feel like I'll get banned from Goodreads if I declare that I think the movies are better than the books, but I'll just say that there's a lot of things that the movies did that improves the clarity of The Lord of the Rings, both with the themes and the actual story.

Title: The Shining (The Shining, #1)
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
When you’re rereading a book and it’s just as good as you remember…

These characters are so good and their strengths and weaknesses are paired and utilized so effectively to increase the emotional tension, mistrust, anger, love, whatever. King’s writing is so punchy and when I read the dialogue I can really picture the characters or an actor preforming those lines. It makes an enjoyable movie in my brain.

My only real complaint is mostly a Stephen King complaint where there’s just too much weird ramblings and side info that sometimes seems like a obtuse advertisement for an airline that hasn’t existed in 40 years, but it kind of adds to the schizophrenia of Jack’s character. But adding a whole backstory for a Zippo lighter as if it’s relevant to know is kind of distracting to the action.

In my memory, this book was basically the same as the movie except with more detail, more party weirdness, more dogman, and the climax was a snowmobile chase. Of course the climax is very different and way better than that and even more cinematic than the movie. Probably my favorite horror novel and a perfect cozy warm book for winter.

Ghost stories can be scary but they’re much more frightening when they turn someone you love and trust into something terrifying. And those newfound horrors are not actually new at all but fringe feelings that have been simmering for years and passed down from father to son to son to son.

Title: Stamped from the Beginning: The Definitive History of Racist Ideas in America
Author: Ibram X. Kendi
My Review:
My main takeaway through the book was that everyone, whether they are segregationists, assimilationists, or anti-racists, are lying hypocrites who are almost always looking out for themselves. And then in the epilogue Kendi says that the only effective way to end discrimination is to make powerful people believe that ending discrimination is in their own self interest; so maybe my reading comprehension skills have not fully rotted away just yet.

As someone who went through the public school system in a conservative area, it's kind of eye-opening to see how much assimilationist rhetoric I was taught. I also remember that in elementary school we were taught that the civil war was fought over the right to own slaves and then by middle school we learned it was actually about states' rights and slavery was just a little part of what states should be able to control. And then in high school we started to develop brains that could actually form their own opinions and we woke up.

I think that the book's organization and pacing is done well and although it's focused on race, Kendi knows that writing a compendium on racist ideas must address gender, sexuality, ethnicity, etc. Kendi's conclusion is a little depressing and could be interpreted as cynical, but it's also actionable and not devoid of hope.

Title: The Overstory
Author: Richard Powers
My Review:
3.5

Interesting to see when trees emerge into the consciousnesses of each of the characters. For some it’s a burden handed down by their fathers that they can’t escape, and for others the revelation arrives much later in life. Only once they’re physically immobilized; in a wheelchair, a jail cell, a bed, do they get the chance to notice.

I was waiting for a concrete message to emerge by the end. What’s the point? But of course the novel never gives us the satisfaction. The book is idealistic enough to have the characters fight wholeheartedly for trees while still undercutting their purpose with internal and external resistance.

The problem/blessing of having so many storylines is that you get every type of ending. An optimistic one, a cathartic one, a hopeless one… And although every person’s story ends a different way, the story of trees stays ongoing.

“People have no idea what time is. They think it’s a line, spinning out from three seconds behind them, then vanishing just as fast into three seconds of fog just ahead. Title: The Covenant of Water
Author: Abraham   Verghese
My Review:
4.5 stars

Every author is a writer but not every author is also a doctor. I don’t usually like books that feature a main character who is an author, but it’s evident that this author is pouring his entire being and life experience into his characters, and Philipose’s writing is a key part of the story so I’ll forgive him. I'm sure that the characters were also informed by the thousands of patients that Verghese has seen over the course of his career as a doctor, and he does a great job at knowing when to explain anatomy literally and when to use metaphor and abstraction.

I don’t know if I’ve ever read a book where I love each character equally in this way. Each death or loss hits like a truck. Every character holds a collection of contradictions; faith, mysticism, and medicine all intertwine in a really beautiful way, and by the end of the book, some things that seem supernatural are explained through science, while others remain inexplicable.

It’s really engaging but it’s sooo long. I was getting tired by the halfway mark but I thought that if I took an extended break from the book, I might forget all of the characters.

I was initially confused at the final familial reveal, but as the last few chapters progressed and it all got explained, my heart broke into a million little pieces.

Big recommendation from me if you wanna train your attention span.

Title: Philosophy 101: From Plato and Socrates to Ethics and Metaphysics, an Essential Primer on the History of Thought (Adams 101 Series)
Author: Paul Kleinman
My Review:
there was only one chapter on eastern philosophy, which included one paragraph on confucianism. and in that one paragraph the author said that "Confucius created the ... notion of Yin Yang". amazing. are u kidding me.

this book is so dry. there are so many unnecessary details but also so much important stuff left out at the same time. i thought philosophy was about thinking for yourself and making your own conclusions; the author does not encourage any of that.

also the chapter order makes no sense at all i'm pretty sure the order is random. there are 54 chapters. the 50th chapter deals with ethics. shouldn't that be one of the first chapters?? i don't understand how it goes Pre-Socratic --> Socrates --> Plato --> Aristotle, which makes perfect, LOGICAL sense, and then jumps to francis bacon, hume, BACK to st. aquinas, flash forward to rousseau, kant, stepping back 100 years to locke, 100 mOre years backwards to descartes and hobbes, then (finally) formally introducing metaphysics (????), followed by jumping 300 years to sartre (-1980), backtracking AGAIN to a chapter on the enlightenment, giving me whiplash by immediately jumping to nietzsche (-1900) in the very next chapter, then introducing epistemology (the study OF KNOWLEDGE) in the 38TH CHAPTER, then schopenhauer and marx and heidegger (all 3 of which are actually in chronological order), immediately followed by voltaire, who lived before all three of those german dudes, and then one chapter on eastern philosophy (couldn't he have broken it up even a little bit?), then going to the year 980 with avicenna, then JUMPING AGAIN all the freaNKINGHTDEONEHUODH way to bertrand russell who died in 1970, then lightly touching on phenomenology, ethics, philosophy of science, spinoza (for some reason being the 2nd to last chapter), before finishing with a chapter on the philosophy of religion. WHY. the nonsense ordering goes to the last chapter. it would make infinitely more sense for the philosophy of religion to be the first chapter instead. why not talk about the future of philosophy at the end?

here is what it says in the book description:
Philosophy 101 cuts out the boring details and exhausting philosophical methodology, and instead, gives you a lesson in philosophy that keeps you engaged as you explore the fascinating history of human thought and inquisition.

incorrect.

since almost everyone reading this book will be new to philosophy, it's important for this book to be engaging, unbiased, and accurate in order to give those reading a good foundation on which to build their philosophical knowledge.

what a terrible fucking booK
